newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Heavy security for Albanian president's visit.
newsitem.headline: Heavy security for Albanian president's visit.

text.p: Albanian police imposed heavy security on Tuesday for a visit by President Sali Berisha to discuss failed pyramid investment schemes which have sparked riots in this town last month.
Plainclothes police swarmed around the town centre. Armed guards were perched on rooftops overlooking the main square and police told drivers they could not park nearby.
Supporters waving the blue flag of the ruling Democratic Party headed for the square but were turned back by police.
Locals said there was little chance people would be able to stage protests, partly because many demonstrators were arrested after violent clashes last month and were still being held.

The town hall was burned in the protests by investors who lost money when five pyramid schemes collapsed. Deputy Prime Minister Tritan Shehu came to the town to explain the collapse and was attacked by an angry crowd.
Shehu accompanied Berisha on his Tuesday visit.
Thousands of investors blame the pro-market government for failing to regulate the schemes, which lured cash with offers of high interest, and for failing to warn them of the risks.
"Nothing is going to happen. Police cracked down on them 10 days ago. Dozens are still being held," said Flamur, 25.
About 2,000 people waited passively by the square for a glimpse of Berisha. Police quickly drove off anyone who tried to talk with foreign reporters at the scene.
Berisha, who arrived in the afternoon in Lushnje, 85 km (53 miles) south of Tirana, will address selected supporters of the ruling right-wing Democrats.
Members of the audience had to show police their personal invitation and their identity cards before entering the central theatre where Berisha was speaking.
The theatre is next to the town hall, which was burned in January by protesters who had lost money in pyramid investment schemes.
It is the second time in four days that Berisha has tried to win support in the face of anti-government protests across the Balkan country.

The Democrats also plan a mass rally in Tirana on Thursday to commemorate February 20, 1991, when the statue of communist dictator Enver Hoxha was toppled. Hoxha ruled Albania with an iron fist for 40 years.

Berisha is struggling to regain support for the free-market government which came to power in 1992. It has faced protests and riots since the popular but fraudulent pyramid saving schemes collapsed last month.

Meanwhile, in Tirana, Albania's last communist leader, Ramiz Alia, was charged with crimes against humanity and genocide. The trial was postponed after Alia's lawyer in the ramshackle courthouse demanded the judges resign because of procedural mistakes.
"The appeals court will rule on your request. I declare the session closed," presiding judge Martin Deda told Alia's lawyer Kleanthi Koci. The ruling was expected within 10 days.
Alia, 72, was the handpicked successor of dictator Hoxha. Four other officials are also on trial, two in absentia.
The prosecutor said the defendants gave shoot-to-kill orders to border guards to stop Albanians from fleeing. If convicted, they face a mimimum penalty of 15 years and a maximum of the death penalty.
